text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Home owners of properties on Sweden's most sought-after coastlines will see taxes increase the most, according to preliminary calculations for next year -- about 17 percent.
- Six small niche banks have appealed to Finance Minister Erik Asbrink over the refusal by larger banks to handle transactions, saying they are faced with unfair competition.
- A sudden freezing in Stockholm on Sunday led to over 100 car accidents. Some 50 people were admitted to hospital.

- Airlines are keeping older planes in service longer as economic competition between different companies increases. Statistics show that the number of planes over 20 years old that are still flying has doubled in the past two years. Fifteen of 35 bad accidents around the year this year involved old planes.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson, recently returned from a trip to China and Hong Kong, says he has had enough of long overseas trips and will spend next year concentrating on domestic affairs.
- Sweden's music exports are a myth with growth in the industry levelling out and the record industry faring badly. Sales over the past nine months have fallen 19 percent to 843 million crowns.

- American investment bank Morgan Stanley says international electrical engineering company ABB and Sweden's tool maker/engineer Sandvik are two of the world's most competitive companies with business leader Percy Barnevik playing a key role in both companies.

- Investment company Custos has sold about 15 million A-shares in S-E-Banken so far this year but still has about five million left. Managing director Marcus Storch said these would also be sold shortly with Custo's new strategy to sell out of companies that it cannot influence.
